analogy.p: Think of a car's speedometer needle as the velocity and a stopwatch as time. Acceleration is how quickly the needle is moving round the dial: a fast-moving needle is a big acceleration, a still needle (even at a high reading) is zero acceleration. A velocity-time graph is a film of the speedometer plotted against time: the slope of the plotted line is how fast the needle is moving, and the area under the line is the odometer reading, the distance covered. It breaks down because a speedometer shows only speed and not direction, whereas a velocity-time graph can go below the axis for travelling backwards, which an ordinary speedometer cannot show.
analogy.t: The speedometer and the car journey

bullets: Acceleration = how quickly velocity changes; it is the change in velocity every second.
Speeding up in the direction of motion: positive acceleration (if that direction is positive).
Slowing down: **deceleration**, which is a negative acceleration when the direction of motion is taken as positive.
Constant velocity (steady speed in a straight line) means zero acceleration.
Changing direction at constant speed (circular motion) also involves acceleration because velocity changes.
Acceleration of 3 m/s2 means velocity increases by 3 m/s every second.
Link: a resultant force on an object causes acceleration (Newton's second law, F = m a) so acceleration is always linked to unbalanced forces.
core.p: **Acceleration** is the rate at which velocity changes. An object accelerates when its velocity changes: it can speed up, slow down, or change direction. Because velocity is a vector, acceleration is also a **vector quantity**, so it has a direction as well as a size. In everyday language 'accelerating' means speeding up, but in physics a car braking, a car turning a corner at constant speed and a ball thrown upwards are all accelerating.

bullets: a = Δv / t = (v - u) / t where v = final velocity and u = initial velocity.
Rearrangements: Δv = a t; t = Δv / a. And v = u + a t.
Units: acceleration m/s2; velocity m/s; time s. Always convert to these units first.
Example: a car going from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 6 s: a = (20 - 8) / 6 = 12 / 6 = 2.0 m/s2.
A negative answer means the velocity is decreasing (or the acceleration is in the negative direction).
If the object starts from rest, u = 0, so a = v / t.
Make sure the change in velocity is final minus initial; swapping them gives the wrong sign.
core.h: The equation a = change in velocity / time
core.p: For an object with uniform (constant) acceleration, **acceleration (m/s2) = change in velocity (m/s) / time taken (s)**, written a = Δv / t. The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity: Δv = v - u. Written in full: a = (v - u) / t. This equation must be recalled and rearranged. The unit m/s2 means 'metres per second, per second': the velocity changes by that many m/s in each second.

bullets: Speeding up in the positive direction: a > 0.
Slowing down while moving in the positive direction: a < 0 (deceleration).
Speeding up in the negative direction (e.g. falling downwards if up is positive): a < 0 as well.
Slowing down while moving in the negative direction: a > 0.
Constant velocity: a = 0, which needs a zero resultant force (Newton's first law).

The sign tells you the direction of the acceleration, not whether the object is 'speeding up'. To decide that, compare the directions of velocity and acceleration: same direction means speeding up; opposite means slowing down.
In exam answers about braking, 'deceleration of 5 m/s2' or 'acceleration of -5 m/s2' are both acceptable.
core.h: Positive, negative and zero acceleration; deceleration
core.p: Acceleration, like velocity, is a vector so we use signs on a straight line. If forward is positive, a vehicle speeding up forwards has positive acceleration. When it brakes, its velocity is still forward but decreasing, so its acceleration is negative; this is called **deceleration**. Zero acceleration means the velocity is constant: the object might be stationary or moving at a steady velocity.

bullets: v2 - u2 = 2 a s where v = final velocity (m/s), u = initial velocity (m/s), a = acceleration (m/s2), s = distance (m).
Starting from rest (u = 0): v2 = 2 a s, so v = square root of (2 a s).
To find a: a = (v2 - u2) / (2 s). To find s: s = (v2 - u2) / (2 a).
Example: starts at rest, a = 3.0 m/s2 over 24 m: v2 = 2 x 3.0 x 24 = 144, so v = 12 m/s.
Example: braking from 30 m/s to rest over 90 m: 0 - 900 = 2 a x 90, so a = -900 / 180 = -5.0 m/s2 (deceleration of 5.0 m/s2).
Only valid for constant acceleration; the exam question usually states 'constant' or 'uniform'.
Common error: forgetting to square v and u, or doing (v - u)2 instead of v2 - u2.
core.h: Uniform acceleration and v2 - u2 = 2 a s
core.p: For **uniform acceleration** (acceleration that stays constant) there is a second equation that connects velocity, acceleration and distance without needing the time: **(final velocity)2 - (initial velocity)2 = 2 x acceleration x distance**, written v2 - u2 = 2 a s. The equation is used when the time is not given or not wanted. Notice the velocities are squared, so you must square before subtracting and take a square root at the end if asked for v.

bullets: Near the Earth's surface g is approximately 9.8 m/s2 (often 10 m/s2 in rough estimates; use the value given in the question).
Velocity of an object dropped from rest: v = g t, so after 1 s it is 9.8 m/s, after 2 s 19.6 m/s, after 3 s 29.4 m/s.
Distance fallen using v2 = 2 g s: after reaching 19.6 m/s, s = 19.6 x 19.6 / (2 x 9.8) = 384.16 / 19.6 = 19.6 m.
All objects accelerate at the same rate in free fall because weight is proportional to mass (W = m g) while the mass in F = m a cancels.
In real situations air resistance matters, especially for light or wide objects such as feathers and parachutes.
On the Moon gravity is weaker (about 1.6 m/s2), so free fall acceleration is smaller.
Link: the weight of an object is W = m g and the resultant force is F = m a.
core.h: Acceleration due to gravity: free fall
core.p: Near the Earth's surface, any object in **free fall** (falling with only its weight acting, so ignoring air resistance) has an acceleration of about **9.8 m/s2** downwards. This value is the gravitational field strength expressed as an acceleration, so g = 9.8 N/kg = 9.8 m/s2. It does not depend on the mass of the object: a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate in a vacuum. In air, resistance reduces the acceleration as speed increases (leading to terminal velocity, the next topic).

bullets: y-axis: velocity (m/s); x-axis: time (s). Always label axes with quantity and unit.
A straight sloping line means uniform (constant) acceleration.
A horizontal line means constant velocity, so zero acceleration.
A line that returns to zero velocity means the object has stopped.
A line below the time axis means the velocity is negative (moving in the opposite direction).
Do not confuse with distance-time graphs, where the gradient gives speed and a horizontal line means stationary.
Describe motion by sections: 'from 0 to 5 s the object accelerates uniformly from rest to 10 m/s'.
core.p: A **velocity-time graph** plots velocity (y-axis, m/s) against time (x-axis, s). It shows how the velocity of an object changes during its motion. Two pieces of information can be extracted from the graph: the **gradient** of the line gives the acceleration and the **area under the line** gives the distance travelled. These two ideas are the most heavily examined skills in this topic.

bullets: Gradient = rise / run = change in velocity / change in time = acceleration (m/s2).
In the figure: 0 to 5 s: gradient = 10 / 5 = +2 m/s2; 5 to 15 s: gradient 0; 15 to 20 s: gradient = -10 / 5 = -2 m/s2.
Steeper line = larger acceleration; shallower line = smaller acceleration.
Negative gradient = negative acceleration (slowing down if velocity is positive).
Use large triangles for accuracy and include units in the answer.
Reading the graph scales: check what each square represents before calculating, as scales are often not 1 square = 1 unit.
Describing it: 'The gradient is zero so there is no acceleration; the object travels at constant velocity.'
core.h: Gradient of a velocity-time graph = acceleration
core.p: The **gradient** of a velocity-time graph is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, which is exactly the definition of acceleration. So **gradient = acceleration**. The steeper the line, the greater the acceleration. A straight line has a constant gradient (uniform acceleration). To calculate it, choose two points on the line that are far apart, draw a triangle, and divide the vertical side (change in v) by the horizontal side (change in t).

bullets: Rectangle: area = base x height = time x constant velocity.
Triangle: area = 1/2 x base x height (for constant acceleration from or to rest).
Trapezium: area = 1/2 x (sum of parallel sides) x height.
Worked in the figure: triangle 1/2 x 5 x 10 = 25 m; rectangle 10 x 10 = 100 m; triangle 25 m; total 150 m (or trapezium 1/2 x (20 + 10) x 10 = 150 m).
Counting squares: if 1 large square is 2 m/s wide and 1 s long then it represents 2 m. Count squares then multiply (Higher tier skill for curves).
Units: area of velocity (m/s) x time (s) gives metres.
Average speed over a journey = total distance (area) / total time.
core.h: Area under a velocity-time graph = distance travelled
core.p: The **area between the line and the time axis** equals the **distance travelled** (displacement if velocities can be negative). This works because distance = velocity x time, and the area of a rectangle on the graph is height (velocity) x width (time). For straight-line graphs split the area into rectangles, triangles and trapezia. For curved graphs you can estimate the area by **counting squares**: work out what one square represents, count the whole squares (and combine part squares), then multiply.

bullets: Tangent: a straight line touching the curve at one point, with the same gradient as the curve at that point.
Acceleration at a point = gradient of the tangent = change in v / change in t for the tangent line.
A curve getting steeper means the acceleration is increasing; a curve flattening means the acceleration is decreasing.
A flattening curve that becomes horizontal means the acceleration has fallen to zero (e.g. terminal velocity).
To draw a good tangent use a ruler, position it so the angle on both sides of the point looks balanced, and use a large triangle.
Estimate distance under a curve by counting squares: count whole squares and treat part-squares as halves roughly.
The higher the point of the graph, the higher the velocity; do not mistake height for acceleration.
core.h: Non-uniform acceleration and curved graphs (Higher tier)
core.p: When the acceleration is not constant the velocity-time graph is a curve. On a curve the gradient changes from point to point. To find the acceleration at a particular instant, draw a **tangent** to the curve at that point (a straight line that just touches the curve and has the same slope) and calculate its gradient. The distance travelled is still the area under the curve, found by counting squares. A curve getting flatter shows decreasing acceleration, as in a falling object approaching terminal velocity.

bullets: Line crossing the axis: velocity is zero at that moment and the direction reverses.
A ball thrown upwards: velocity positive and decreasing to zero at the top, then negative as it falls, with constant gradient of -9.8 m/s2 throughout if air resistance is ignored.
Displacement = (area above axis) - (area below axis); distance = (area above) + (area below).
Gradient is still the acceleration: a straight line crossing the axis has constant acceleration the whole time.
Example: a trolley moving at +4 m/s that slows uniformly and returns at -4 m/s has a constant negative gradient.
Always check the sign of velocity before saying 'speeding up' or 'slowing down'.
Use correct phrases like 'moving back towards the start' when velocity is negative.
core.p: If a velocity-time graph crosses the time axis the object changes direction. The part above the axis represents motion in the positive direction and the part below represents motion in the negative direction. The area above gives positive displacement and the area below gives negative displacement. The total displacement is the area above minus the area below (in size), but the total distance travelled adds the sizes of both areas.

bullets: Axes: time on x, velocity on y, units in labels (time / s, velocity / m/s).
Choose scales that use at least half of the graph paper and are easy to read (1, 2, 5 or 10 per square).
Plot points to within half a small square, then draw a line of best fit or smooth curve.
For gradient: choose two points on the line far apart, read values, divide change in v by change in t.
For area: split into simple shapes and add.
Check units and the sensible size of your answer, e.g. cars rarely accelerate at more than 5 m/s2.
Comparing graphs: a steeper gradient for car A means A has greater acceleration than B; a higher line means higher velocity, not greater acceleration.
core.h: Drawing and interpreting velocity-time graphs: skills
core.p: Questions often give a table of times and velocities and ask you to plot a graph, or give a graph and ask for an acceleration or a distance. Draw axes using at least half the grid, choose a sensible scale (such as 1 cm per 1 s), label with quantity and unit, plot points accurately as small crosses, and draw a straight line with a ruler (if the points follow a straight trend) or a smooth curve. Then extract the gradient or area as required.

bullets: Distance-time graph: gradient = speed; horizontal = stopped; straight sloping = constant speed; curve = changing speed.
Velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration; horizontal = constant velocity; area = distance.
Horizontal line on a v-t graph does NOT mean the object has stopped unless the line is at zero velocity.
Link to F = m a: acceleration from the graph gives the resultant force when the mass is known.
Link to terminal velocity: the v-t graph curves and flattens as resultant force falls to zero.
Link to stopping distances: braking is a negative-gradient section; the area gives the braking distance.
Link to energy: kinetic energy depends on v2, so doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy and also the braking distance for the same deceleration.
core.p: It is vital not to mix up the two types of graph. On a **distance-time graph** the gradient is speed (or velocity), a horizontal line means stationary, and a curve with increasing gradient means acceleration. On a **velocity-time graph** the gradient is acceleration, a horizontal line means constant velocity, and the area gives distance. Acceleration links forward to Newton's second law, stopping distances, momentum and terminal velocity.

exam: Command words: 'calculate' (equation, substitution, answer with unit); 'describe the motion' (state what happens in each section, with values); 'explain' (link cause and effect, e.g. 'resultant force is zero so acceleration is zero').
Equation marks: a = (v - u) / t is recalled (1 mark), substitution (1), answer (1), unit m/s2 (1). v2 - u2 = 2as is selected from the equation sheet and applied.
Graph-reading 2-mark pattern: choose two points on the line (1) and divide change in velocity by change in time (1) with units.
Area pattern: split into shapes (1), correct areas (1), sum with unit metres (1). Show each shape's calculation clearly.
'Describe' answers must use numbers: 'accelerates uniformly from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s, then constant velocity of 10 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s'.
Never write that the object 'stops' when the line is horizontal above zero; say 'travels at constant velocity'.
For 6-mark questions combine calculation and explanation: gradient for acceleration, area for distance, and link to forces (resultant force = mass x acceleration).
Higher tier: draw a tangent with a ruler and use a large triangle; marks are often given for a correct tangent (1), triangle values (1) and answer within tolerance (1).
Counting squares: state what one square represents, count whole and part squares, then multiply. Examiners allow a range.
Check answers: typical car acceleration is 2 to 3 m/s2, braking 5 to 8 m/s2, free fall 9.8 m/s2. An answer of 200 m/s2 for a car is wrong.
Give a negative sign or the word deceleration to describe slowing down; marks are lost for a negative distance or area.
Use 2 or 3 significant figures and show working so error-carried-forward marks can be awarded.

mistakes.r: The gradient of a v-t graph is acceleration (speed is the gradient of a distance-time graph).
mistakes.w: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is speed.

mistakes.r: It means constant velocity (zero acceleration); stationary only if the line is at v = 0.
mistakes.w: A horizontal line on a v-t graph means the object is stationary.

mistakes.r: Acceleration = change in velocity / time, a = (v - u) / t.
Use the area under the line (triangle, rectangle or trapezium), or use average velocity x time.
mistakes.w: Calculating distance from a v-t graph as velocity x total time when the line slopes.

mistakes.r: State 'deceleration of 5 m/s2' or 'acceleration of -5 m/s2' clearly.
mistakes.w: Writing a deceleration as a positive number with no explanation, or ignoring the sign.

mistakes.r: Square v and u separately then subtract: v2 - u2.
Without air resistance all objects have the same acceleration, 9.8 m/s2.
mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster in free fall.

mistakes.r: For acceleration at a point, draw a tangent at that point (Higher tier).
mistakes.w: Reading the gradient triangle on a curve using any chord.

mistakes.r: A steeper line means a larger acceleration; a higher line means a larger velocity.
mistakes.w: A steeper line means a higher velocity.

mistakes.r: Convert to seconds and give m/s2 for acceleration.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or leaving time in minutes.

summary: The specification asks you to recall and use acceleration = change in velocity / time, to use v2 - u2 = 2as for uniform acceleration, to know that free fall near Earth's surface has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s2, and to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs, using the gradient to find acceleration and the area to find distance (including tangents and counting squares for curves at Higher tier). It underpins Newton's laws, terminal velocity and stopping distances.

terms.d: The rate of change of velocity; change in velocity divided by time taken; a vector quantity measured in m/s2.
A negative acceleration; the rate at which an object slows down.
Acceleration that stays constant over time.
A graph of velocity (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for a moving object.
The slope of a line: change in the y-axis quantity divided by change in the x-axis quantity.
A straight line that touches a curve at a point and has the same gradient as the curve there.
The velocity of an object at the start of the time considered.
The velocity of an object at the end of the time considered.
Motion of an object falling under the influence of gravity alone, with no other forces acting.
About 9.8 m/s2 near the Earth's surface; the acceleration of a freely falling object.
Metres per second squared: the unit of acceleration, the change in velocity in m/s each second.
The distance travelled (displacement) in the time interval.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object; it causes acceleration.
A quantity with both size and direction; acceleration is a vector.
Steady speed in a fixed direction; the acceleration is zero.

worked.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 8.0 m/s to 20 m/s in 6.0 s. Calculate its acceleration. [3 marks]
steps: a = change in velocity / time = 12 / 6.0 (1 mark).

worked.q: (a) A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3.0 m/s2 over a distance of 24 m. Calculate her final velocity. (b) A car travelling at 30 m/s brakes uniformly to rest in a distance of 90 m. Calculate its acceleration. [6 marks]
steps: v = square root of 144 = 12 m/s (1 mark).
(b) 0 - 30 squared = 2 x a x 90, so -900 = 180 a (1 mark).
a = -5.0 m/s2, a deceleration of 5.0 m/s2 (1 mark).

worked.q: A train's velocity-time graph is a straight line from 0 to 10 m/s over the first 5 s, then horizontal at 10 m/s until 15 s, then a straight line down to 0 m/s at 20 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration in the first 5 s. (b) Calculate the total distance. (c) Calculate the average speed. [7 marks]
steps: Triangle 1: 1/2 x 5 x 10 = 25 m; rectangle: 10 x 10 = 100 m; triangle 2: 1/2 x 5 x 10 = 25 m (2 marks).
Total distance = 25 + 100 + 25 = 150 m (1 mark). Check with trapezium: 1/2 x (20 + 10) x 10 = 150 m.
(c) Average speed = total distance / total time = 150 / 20 (1 mark) = 7.5 m/s (1 mark).
